title: Stability of the Gauss fraction field of a Tate algebra
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], complete for a nontrivial real-valued multiplicative nonarchimedean absolute value, and stable in the sense of [def-trf-stable-nonarchimedean-field]. Let $e\ge0$ and $T=k\langle U_1,\ldots,U_eangle$ be the restricted-series ring [def-trf-restricted-series-presentation], with $G(\sum_
u a_
u U^
u)=\sup_
u|a_
u|$. Then $T$ is an integral domain, $G$ is multiplicative, and the formula $|a/b|_F=G(a)/G(b)$, for $a,b\in T$ and $b
e0$, defines a real-valued multiplicative nonarchimedean absolute value on $F=\operatorname{Frac}(T)$ extending that of $k$. With this absolute value, $F$ is stable [def-trf-stable-nonarchimedean-field]. No completeness of $F$ is asserted.

source.place: Proposition 5.1.2/1, printed p.193 (scan PDF p.199), and Stability Theorem 5.3.2/1, printed p.213 (scan PDF p.219). Primary scan read 2026-10-24; e=0 is the identity case.

proof.text: If $e=0$, the restricted-series ring consists of constants, so $T=k$, $G=|\cdot|_k$ and $F=k$; every assertion is the given field and stability hypothesis [def-trf-stable-nonarchimedean-field]. Hence assume $e\ge1$. By [lem-trf-restricted-series-gauss-completion] the coefficient supremum is finite, definite, invariant under negation, normalized at $1$ and ultrametric. By [lem-trf-tate-gauss-multiplicative], $G(ab)=G(a)G(b)$. If $ab=0$ and both factors were nonzero, definiteness would give $0=G(a)G(b)>0$. Constants give $1\ne0$, so $T$ is an integral domain.

source.place: Proposition 5.1.2/1, printed p.193; zero-variable case from the definitions.

proof.text: Define $|a/b|_F=G(a)/G(b)$ for $b\ne0$. Its denominator is positive. If $a/b=c/d$, then $ad=cb$, and multiplicativity gives $G(a)G(d)=G(c)G(b)$, proving independence of representatives. For products, $G(ac)/G(bd)=(G(a)/G(b))(G(c)/G(d))$. For sums, $$\frac{G(ad+cb)}{G(bd)}\le\frac{\max(G(a)G(d),G(c)G(b))}{G(b)G(d)}=\max\left(\frac{G(a)}{G(b)},\frac{G(c)}{G(d)}\right).$$ Definiteness follows from $a/b=0\iff a=0$; normalization and negation follow from those of $G$. For a constant $u$, $G(u)=|u|_k$, so the fraction norm extends the given absolute value and is nontrivial. This verifies every absolute-value axiom directly.

source.place: Proposition 5.1.2/1, printed p.193, extended to fractions by the displayed calculation.

proof.text: Let $P\subset T$ be the subring of finite-support coefficient families, namely the polynomial ring in the $U_i$, and let $R\subset F$ be its fraction field. The coefficient embedding is injective and preserves multiplication; its norm is the maximum of its finitely many coefficient absolute values. Thus the restricted absolute value on $R$ is exactly the Gauss absolute value in [lem-trf-gauss-rational-function-stability]. That node applies because $k$ is complete, nontrivially valued and stable and $e\ge1$, and proves that $R$ is stable. Here $R$ is the rational function field, not the fraction field of all restricted series.

source.place: Sections 5.3.3–5.3.4, concluding paragraph printed p.220; reduction described in Section 5.3.2, printed p.214.

proof.text: For $a/b\in F$, $b\ne0$, let $p_N,q_N\in P$ be the total-degree truncations of $a,b$. They converge in $G$ by [lem-trf-restricted-series-gauss-completion]. For all sufficiently large $N$, $G(q_N-b)<G(b)$, whence the two ultrametric inequalities imply $G(q_N)=G(b)>0$. Moreover $G(p_N)\le G(a)$ because truncation removes coefficients. The identity $$\frac ab-\frac{p_N}{q_N}=\frac{(a-p_N)q_N+p_N(q_N-b)}{bq_N}$$ therefore gives $$\left|\frac ab-\frac{p_N}{q_N}\right|_F\le\max\left(\frac{G(a-p_N)}{G(b)},\frac{G(a)G(q_N-b)}{G(b)^2}\right)\longrightarrow0.$$ Thus $R$ is dense in $F$, with exactly the isometric inclusion of step 3. The calculation also covers $a=0$.

source.place: Section 5.3.2, paragraph preceding Proposition 3, printed p.214; explicit rational-truncation estimate supplied here.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-tate-fraction-weak-stability] to the present $k,T,F$. Its assumptions require completeness and nontriviality of $k$, both given; it requires neither stability of $k$ nor separability of a finite extension. Consequently every finite spectral extension of $F$ has the two-sided coordinate-norm bounds displayed there. Together with the stable dense valued subfield $R$ from steps 3–4, these are exactly the hypotheses of [lem-trf-dense-weak-stability-transfer] with $K=R$. It follows that $F$ is stable. This conclusion concerns the spectral norm on every finite extension and asserts no completeness of $F$.

source.place: Theorem 5.3.1/1 and Proposition 5.3.2/3, printed pp.212–214; completion criterion Proposition 3.6.2/3, printed p.158.
